title: CrowdStrike buys missing network security piece in $43.9B Zscaler deal
raw_text: CrowdStrike agreed to acquire cloud security company Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal on Monday, combining endpoint protection with zero-trust network security in one of the largest cybersecurity acquisitions ever and intensifying the industry’s race to build broad security platforms. The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio. While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and zero-trust network access platform. “With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment,” CrowdStrike said in a statement. The companies expect the deal to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal 2028, subject to approval by Zscaler shareholders and regulators, the statement added. The deal is larger than Google’s $32 billion purchase of Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk , both completed earlier this year. From partnership to one platform CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz framed the deal around AI in the statement. “With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” Kurtz said. Yih Khai Wong, research director at IDC, said the deal fits a pattern of larger security vendors “buying into adjacent control points rather than building them organically.” Until now, he said, CrowdStrike “lacks a strong, owned network/SSE layer.” The two companies are not starting from scratch. The statement described the relationship as one of CrowdStrike’s largest technology alliances, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations. CrowdStrike argued that a partnership integrates separate products, while one company integrates “the data, the roadmap, the go-to-market, and the commercial model.” Wong said the existing partnership already delivers much of the correlation value. Ownership adds “control over the roadmap and the pace of integration,” he said. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the merger buys “fluency rather than new vocabulary.” One owner means a single data model and faster correlation, he said, but that gain is “narrower than any merger pitch will claim.” He advised CISOs to ask the vendors to show, in their own environments, which outcomes today’s integration cannot already reach. One contract, one renewal The commercial plan is central to the deal. After closing, customers of either company will be able to buy the other’s products on a single Falcon Flex contract, the statement said. CrowdStrike identified about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not yet use CrowdStrike, and said it expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing. “Falcon Flex will bring Zscaler onto the commercial model customers already use, so they commit once and expand from there,” the statement said. Gogia said that model shifts leverage over time. “Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second,” he said. The second signature comes at renewal, he said, when the supplier holds more of the estate and the buyer holds fewer alternatives. He advised CFOs and CISOs to price consolidation offers at their first full renewal, and to keep one credible alternative alive in each layer they consolidate. Wong said consolidation “addresses real integration challenges for enterprises that commit to a single platform, while quietly reducing the leverage and flexibility of those that don’t.” Enterprises in heavily regulated industries that need best-of-breed tools may find bundled platforms fall short, he added. Two layers, one release train CrowdStrike also expects $500 million in annualized cost synergies within 18 to 24 months of closing, mainly from optimizing data center infrastructure, vendors and operations, the statement said. For security teams, the question is whether that consolidation reaches the products themselves. Today the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds, with separate release schedules, Gogia said. “A merged agent, a shared update pipeline, or a single control plane would change that,” Gogia said. “One bad release would then reach the device and the way in together.” Wong said CISOs should build that scenario into their business continuity plans, since “an incident could affect both the endpoint agent and the access control plane.” Gogia advised teams to map every access rule that depends on CrowdStrike’s device posture check, and to keep a fallback route that relies on neither vendor. Customers that pair Zscaler with another endpoint product, or Falcon with another SSE provider, should get integration commitments in writing, he said. “Neutrality promised in a blog post lasts exactly as long as the blog post.” Until the deal closes, both companies will continue to operate independently, the statement added.

The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio.

title: Clever AI prompt ideas every security leader should steal
raw_text: For all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expediate tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making, and potentially save big on auditing. Several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development, and critical thinking. Developing truly useful prompts isn’t particularly easy, however, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. Fortunately, the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making, and saving time for hands-on defense. Create an adversarial assistant to control damage — and cut down AI slop Dzmitry Romanovadvocates establishing an AI prompt that acts as a second security reviewer to help catch latent problems before any damage occurs. The key, though, is to give it an adversarial twist so that it looks at a situation from the attacker’s perspective while critiquing the human security reviewer’s ideas. “What am I missing? What attack vectors or edge cases should I inspect?” is the kind of questions Romanov, cybersecurity team lead and senior security engineer at the Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics and cybersecurity team lead with Vention, an AI-enabled software development company, such a prompt can help with. “This approach works most effectively when analyzing architecture or code, while reviewing penetration test results, and auditing cloud configurations, as well as when modeling threats and assessing risks,” Romanov says. Philippe Dourassov, AI pentest lead at Aikido Security, offers another version of the adversarial agent prompt — in this case against agent helpers. When agents are used to generate security reports, engineers often find themselves buried under irrelevant findings — noise, says Dourassov. However, when a second agent is deployed to analyze the quality of another agent’s work, and correct its output, the result can be surprisingly efficient. “The first agent has been given a task and will do everything it can to convince the humans that its results are relevant and critical, as this is what the agent would consider a good job,” Dourassov says, noting that his adversarial agent is basically a reviewer. “Its task is to eliminate noise, rectify claims, and highlight the true importance of the first agent’s result.” The agent’s definition of a good job, Dourassov says, is being able to eliminate noise and supply only signal to the human user. “Therefore, it’s essential to use an adversarial prompt to review agents’ output, so we ensure we don’t face security fatigue from AI slop.” Take care of business Brandyn Fisher, senior penetration testing technical lead at business and technology consulting firm Centric Consulting, offers three prompt ideas that CISOs can deploy on a regular basis to aid with their work. The first Fisher uses is a vendor due diligence prompt. “I feed it our organization’s risk thresholds and the vendor in question, and it benchmarks that vendor, sweeps the Internet for security pages, breach history, customer reviews, complaints, and recent news, then returns a structured report I can review and validate quickly,” he explains. Fisher also recommends crafting a professional writing prompt that takes technical analysis and reframes it into language a CIO or board will actually engage with. Gen AI pioneer Kevin Surace offered a similar prompt idea to attendees of this year’s CSO Conference and Awards in May. “Translate the SOC for the boardroom. This is important. They don’t really understand what’s going on,” Surace said. “The prompt here: ‘You are writing the cyber risk section of the board deck. You have four minutes of board time. Below is ninety days of security operations data. Produce three slides for a board that does not know what lateral movement means.’ This is so useful.” Fisher’s third prompt for CISOs is a tech debt reduction prompt “where I list our technology stack and have AI flag underutilized tools, overlapping capabilities, and consolidation opportunities,” he says. Fisher advises building each of his recommendations as a standing agent, project, or skill, or whatever your AI platform supports, so you have a static, repeatable spot to run it instead of rewriting the prompt from scratch every time. Don’t wait for a perfect first version, Fisher adds. “Get an initial prompt working, even if it’s rough, and have AI help draft the instructions themselves.” Expect to revise it several times before it’s reliable. Challenge your policies and content At the CSO Conference, Surace also highlighted how CISOs can use AI prompts to audit their policy libraries. “You are a compliance auditor. I am giving you our policy library and the current text of NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001:2022 Annex A, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05, and the EU AI Act. Produce three lists,” his example prompt began, directing the LLM to find contradictions, gaps, and stale language — the kind of analysis big firms do for six figures in 12 weeks, he noted. Olivia Brännlund, CISO at Outpost24, a cybersecurity and risk management firm, regularly uses a similar prompt that turns AI into an internal auditor and security advisor. The tool reviews policy, processes, risk assessment, incident reports, contract clauses, and specific customer requirements. Brännlund believes that organizations that treat AI as an expert reviewer typically obtain more value than organizations that treat it as a content generator. The key, she states, “isn’t using AI to write content, but using it to challenge content.” Tying together policy review and the adversarial assistant concept, Surace advised CSO conference attendees to also “red team your own runbook.” “You are the operations lead for Scattered Spider. I am giving you our incident response playbook, our detection coverage matrix, and our on-call tree. Identify the five places this runbook fails,” his prompt started, probing for wrong assumptions, bottlenecks, escalation path weaknesses, and so on. “It’s totally worth doing this,” he said. “You will have more information in an hour than you, than you’ve ever had. Vet your agent’s capabilities and weaknesses Chris Hughes advises asking your model what your AI agents can actually do. “Give it an agent’s configuration, tool manifest, or MCP server definitions and ask it to summarize the agent’s effective permissions, the blast radius if it’s compromised, and whether a human approval step exists anywhere in the workflow,” says Hughes, who teaches in the CISO and Leading Enterprise Agentic AI Development Certificate Program at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College. “Most organizations are deploying agents faster than they’re documenting what those agents can reach, and this closes the gap in minutes.” The model turns work that normally requires a senior architect into something an analyst can run at design review, before deployment, and after every change. It also surfaces assumptions the team stopped questioning, Hughes says. The model doesn’t share your blind spots, so it tends to flag the over-permissioned tool or the missing approval gate that everyone walked past, he notes. Once tuned, the prompt becomes a control in its own right rather than a one-off exercise. title: Britain’s data sharing plans should be judged by who they help
raw_text:
Since February, every petrol station in the UK has had to report pump price changes within 30 minutes. The prices go into a free government feed that comparison apps and sat navs use to show drivers the cheapest fuel nearby, and the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) reckons that shopping around can save up to £9 on a tank of fuel. Most commentators have treated Fuel Finder as a cost-of-living measure, with few mentioning that it is an early scheme in a much larger government programme.

That programme is called “smart data,” and it covers two kinds of information. The first is business information like prices and locations, published openly so that app developers can build services with it, as they now do with pump prices. The second is personal records, which a company passes onto another provider of the customer’s choosing, with their permission. The Data (Use and Access) Act lets ministers extend this approach to energy, property, transport and retail, and the government wants at least twenty schemes running by 2035. The call for evidence on which sectors will come next closed in early October; however, a target counted on schemes says little about whether people will use them.

In the 2010s, a voluntary scheme called midata let bank customers download their account history as a spreadsheet, in the hope they would use it to find better deals. Few people wanted to download spreadsheets of their own spending and then upload them to comparison sites, and the CMA later found that usage was very low. A few banks, including HSBC and Santander, still offer the download option, but most people now share their banking data through open banking, making the manual process largely redundant. The right to share the data had existed for years, but almost no one used it until it became much easier.

  • Why open data is needed in the battle to address homelessness: Centrepoint needed to send FOIs to more than 300 local authorities in England to access required information.

Open banking made sharing automatic when it arrived in 2018 through an EU payments law, PSD2, which required banks to let licensed firms access customer accounts with permission, and a CMA order that made Britain’s largest banks build common standards for doing so. Even so, the mass switching of current accounts that regulators anticipated never happened. Instead, people took up open banking through budgeting apps and challenger banks such as Monzo, which gave them good reasons to share, and it now has more than 17 million users.

However, a legal right and working technology still do not guarantee use, as Australia found out after legislating a data right covering its whole economy in 2019. It launched a scheme in banking, where customers could share data but not act on it, for example, by moving money or switching accounts. A review by the Australian Treasury found that strict limits on sharing the data held back new services from developing. By 2023, according to research by the country’s banks, only 0.31% of customers were using it, after the industry had spent around A$1.5 billion.

Brazil’s banking customers had a very different experience. The country’s central bank made participation compulsory for the largest institutions and tied data sharing to Pix (the instant payment system millions of people already used) from the beginning. By September this year, Brazil had counted 269 million active data sharing consents.

The UK’s Fuel Finder follows similar principles on a small scale, since every forecourt has to take part and the prices reach drivers through apps they already use. Registration has reached around 97% of petrol stations so far. Its weak point has been data quality, with What Car?  reporting that several apps showed out-of-date prices that could leave regular users up to £260 a year worse off. Whether it has brought prices down for consumers overall will be clear only when the CMA reports this autumn.

What this tells us is that the next schemes will need compulsory participation, accurate data, and a route to people through services they already use. Home buying is a good candidate, with buyers and sellers already relying on conveyancers and estate agents to chase documents (often in interminable circles) between councils, lenders and the Land Registry. A scheme that compels these bodies to share verified records would reach people through companies they already use, and costly delays in buying and selling property give consumers a reason to want it. A digital property pack from Moverly and the Open Property Data Association, which won the Smart Data Challenge Prize, shows what such a scheme could do. However, it has so far been tested only on synthetic data, but in October, the Open Property Coalition announced that it will test digital property IDs and ways to share property data securely.

Unlike Fuel Finder, schemes in most other sectors will rely on a trade in which customers share their records for faster decisions and/or cheaper products. The government is already consulting on rules that would require energy companies to share certain data with authorised services when customers choose to share it. The risk is that sharing becomes compulsory in name only.

A lender, insurer or energy supplier does not have to refuse customers who keep their data private if it can simply charge them more, reserving its best prices for those who hand over their records. People who can afford the higher price will keep their privacy, and everyone else will pay with their data.

The government’s strategy sets aside one per cent of the smart data budget for monitoring and evaluation, mainly to track growth. As the ODI urged in our response to the recent smart data consultation, it should also show who benefits by publishing how many people use each scheme, what they save and who is charged more for declining to share. Fuel Finder asks drivers for nothing, and there are no penalties for ignoring it. Every scheme should meet the same standard: people use services because they get a better deal, and there are no punitive consequences for saying “no.”

Josh D’Addario is head of consultancy, the Open Data Institute (ODI), which is a member of the UK Smart Data Council.

title: UK Sovereign AI Fund invests in defence tech startup
raw_text:
The UK government’s Sovereign AI Fund and the National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF) have invested in Agon, a company developing the infrastructure needed to train, validate and orchestrate autonomous defence systems. Among the infrastructure the company hopes to develop are artificial intelligence (AI) tools that are designed to defend against drone attacks, as well as a way to ensure AI continues to work as intended if communications are disrupted by an adversary.

Agon is also building a “virtual battlefield” where AI models can be tested cost-effectively against realistic simulations of the situations they might encounter.

The Sovereign AI fund is part of a wider government effort to support British AI innovators and founders to help them develop capabilities that would enable the UK to avoid being too heavily reliant on technology from overseas providers. The National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF) invests in dual-use technologies that strengthen the UK’s national security and defence.

By backing innovative companies developing strategically important capabilities, the government said NSSIF helps enhance the nation’s security, resilience and technological advantage. It said the investment in Agon reflects a continued commitment to technologies with clear national security relevance and the potential to deliver lasting impact.

Agon is one of a number of companies being supported to develop and support home-grown technology and AI capabilities.

Junaid Hussain, co-founder of Agon, said: “Europe cannot afford to outsource the foundational AI capabilities on which its future security will depend. Agon was born out of a project to bring together a coalition of European founders, operators, researchers, veterans, investors and governments to build what we collectively believe to be urgently needed for our sovereignty and safety.”

During the Autumn Budget, the chancellor announced an additional £140m backing for the Sovereign AI Fund. The chancellor also announced that sovereign AI would expand into a new focus area of physical and industrial AI, building on the UK’s leading research base and growing strengths in areas such as robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing.

Sovereign AI investor Will Bushby said: “Defence AI is too important to leave to others. It’s not enough for the UK and Europe to be able to deploy this technology, we need to be able to build it too.”

Discussing the investment, AI minister Kanishka Narayan said: “AI is rapidly transforming how wars are fought, from the use of drones through to how rapidly soldiers can interpret battlefield information. The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era.

“Britain is well-placed to lead efforts to ensure these technologies are reliable, trustworthy and deployed responsibly. Agon’s work will make a valuable contribution to this work: not just British-made AI that our military can use to keep us safe, but defence AI that’s been built in the right way.”

Tristam Constant, co-founder and CEO of Agon, said: “Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare: intelligent agents and machines that will need to understand their environment, make decisions and adapt at a speed and scale that humans alone cannot match. We exist to build the sovereign infrastructure and AI foundation models to allow us to train, test and evolve autonomous defence systems – in Europe, for Europe – to outperform adversary capabilities.”

Based in London and with a second office in Berlin, the company has raised a total of $100m to date.

title: Staff gagging clauses lifted for review of ‘toxic culture’ at information watchdog
raw_text:
Current and former staff of the UK’s information watchdog the Information Commission’s Office (ICO) will have non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) lifted to allow them to contribute to an independent review into the culture, accountability and governance at the organisation.

The review follows the resignation of the information commissioner, John Edwards, in June following allegations of sexual harassment and bullying, leaving a gap in the organisation’s senior leadership that has yet to be filled.

Edwards acknowledged that his conduct fell below the high standards required of leaders in public life, saying there were occasions when “he exercised poor judgement” and had “made attempts at humour that were inappropriate”.

The Information Commission is responsible for regulating data protection and freedom of information and has issued more than £17m fines over the past year, including a £12m fine against TikTok for data protection breaches, including failures to lawfully use children’s data.

Ministers, as first reported by the BBC, are expected to announce details of an independent review into the culture, accountability and governance at the Information Commission this week.

Internal problems

Multiple ICO sources have told Computer Weekly that the regulator’s internal problems extended beyond Edwards to the wider senior leadership at the Information Commission, who were aware of Edwards’ conduct but failed to protect staff.

The Information Commission has entered into 16 non-disclosure agreements with current or former members of staff at a cost of £354,000 since January 2020, according to  disclosures under the Freedom of Information Act (FoI). Nine of the agreements included clauses to prevent employees making disparaging comments about their former employer.

Lawrence Dunne, industrial officer at the Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS), speaking on the BBC’s Today programme on Saturday, said that he hoped the lifting of the NDA’s would allow the review to get at the truth.

“It’s something that PCS has been calling for consistently for some time – that the voice of both the current and former ICO staff who have been the victim of a toxic culture for too long are heard, so we can get to the full truth of the extent of the issues that have been going on,” he added.

He said that compared to other government departments, the Information Commission had issued a large number of NDA agreements. “It really is disturbing that we found that so many have been signed over such a short period of time,” he added.

Staff experienced bullying and harassment

Computer Weekly previously reported that an ICO staff survey this year found that almost one in four employees had experienced or witnessed bullying, harassment or discrimination in the previous 12 months, with more than a third of the incidents involving senior staff. Only 34% of employees said they felt safe speaking up or challenging the way things are done in the organisation.

Following Edward’s resignation, the former technology secretary, Liz Kendall, announced on 8 July that the government would launch an independent review into the culture, accountability and governance of the Information Commission.

Wynne Parry, National Officer at the FDA union, which represents managers and professionals in the public sector, said that the union had been pressing for the independent review since Kendall’s announcement.

“The review needs to be truly independent if it is to gain the confidence of the Commission staff, and the investigation needs to be able to speak freely with those who wish to bring their experience forward,” he added. “We welcome the decision to lift gagging orders so that current and ex-staff can contribute.”

Review should look at resources

Ken Macdonald, former head of ICO Regions, told Computer Weekly that lifting NDA restrictions may be uncomfortable for long-serving members of the existing leadership team but was a necessary step.

“I’m delighted that the gags are to be lifted and, with the implication from that, that former members of staff will be able to feed into the investigation. For them not to would only diminish the investigation’s findings, but the lifting of the non-derogatory elements of NDAs could bring a whole new dimension to the investigation,” he added.

Macdonald said that management and administrative layers in the Information Commission had grown leaving fewer resources for the Information Commission’s core regulatory work.  

“The case backlogs alone tell a story and make a mockery of even the softest of regulatory actions being taken when the Commission isn’t meeting regulatory requirements itself,” he said. “An independent root-and-branch review of its corporate structures is needed and should follow the initial investigation.”

He said that he was concerned that resources for the ICO’s work in the regions had been reduced, with the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish public affairs teams having to manage with fewer staff.

Vulgar and sexualised language

Following Edward’s resignation, former technology secretary Kendall wrote in a post on LinkedIn that an internal investigation had found that the information commissioner’s conduct had fallen short of the standards expected.

“I have seen evidence of the vulgar and highly sexualised language that was used in his interactions with his staff and am extremely concerned that he continues to describe these incidents as misplaced humour,” she said in the statement. “Multiple women shared testimony to the investigator on feeling offended, shocked and uncomfortable following interactions with Mr Edwards.”

A spokesperson from the Department of Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), which oversees the Information Commission, confirmed that the watchdog will not use the terms of any non-disclosure agreements to prevent people from participating in the review.

“An independent review of culture, accountability and governance at the Information Commission is going ahead. We will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly,” the spokesperson added.

ICO ‘committed to learning’

The Information Commission said that it was committed to listening and learning from the events of the past years.

A spokesperson said: “We have never used confidentiality agreements to silence anybody from speaking out about bullying or harassment and we will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the upcoming independent review.

“John Edwards’s conduct was unacceptable and fell well short of the standards we expect, and of the safe, respectful working environment every member of staff deserves. Our new noard, appointed this summer, has been working exceptionally hard to provide fresh leadership, ushering in a new governance structure and a new strategy. It is committed to listening carefully to the review’s findings and recommendations, and building on the positive work on our culture already taking place across the organisation.”

The organisation was restructured on 2 October to bring it in line with other regulators, with responsibility for making decisions now being vested in a board, rather than an individual commissioner.

The Information Commission appointed seven non-executive members in July 2026, who will now play a role in the organisation’s governance strategy.

The regulator is in the process of appointing a new chair, who is expected to take up post in spring 2027.

title: Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez resigns over botched contract
raw_text:
Capita’s CEO will not get to fix the company’s Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) work as he steps down as a consequence of the botched contract.

The company’s share price tanked on news of profits falling by over 50% on Monday 23 November. Extra Capita spending related to trying to fix the CSPS will see profits reduced by over £90m, the firm said.

Capita’s heavy reliance on the UK public sector, combined with its mistakes on the CSPS and the current government’s policy to insource more business, will put the company under pressure.

Adolfo Hernandez, who has had to face public scrutiny as a result of Capita’s disastrous running of the CSPS, will be replaced by chief financial officer Pablo Andres.

Hernandez earned £1.6m in his last pay packet, while thousands of retired civil servants on a pension scheme run by Capita were, as a result of its mistakes, forced to apply for emergency loans.

Capita said in a statement: “The board and Adolfo Hernandez have agreed that Adolfo will step down as CEO and as a member of the board with immediate effect.”

One CSPS member said: “There are interesting reactions on Facebook. Most are elated [that Hernandez is going] but a few are concerned about the risks if Capita collapses completely.”

Hernandez criticised internally

In August, as revealed by Computer Weekly, Hernandez was slammed via an internal message board after making claims that the “right” things are in place to turn the CSPS administration around. The comments from a staff member cast doubt on Capita’s ability to fix the problems being experienced by members of the pension scheme.

In a response to a Hernandez statement, copied to all Capita staff, a member of the pensions team said: “The service provided by Capita surpasses your assertion of ‘not good enough’, it has been abysmal for members. The fact members have died in waiting due to this whole catastrophe is a really harrowing thought that none of us should have to live with, yet we sadly do.”

The worker said that staff have been trying to air their concerns about the CSPS contract, but that all contacts have been “met with vague, deflective and meaningless responses”.

Former civil servant and CSPS member Steve Tessier said: “Glad to see that there is at least some accountability at last.”

Pointing towards the Cabinet Office’s role in the pension scheme disaster, he added: “There are plenty of others who should be getting a P45, too, and not just people from Capita.”

Reacting to Hernandez’s exit, the Civil Service Campaigns Group, made up of people affected by pension delays, said: “Hernandez was CEO throughout this crisis and must be held accountable for Capita’s failures. We repeatedly raised serious concerns directly with him and his senior leadership team, including the devastating impact on members, yet saw little evidence of meaningful action.

“His departure must not be allowed to draw a line under these failures. He, Capita’s board and the Cabinet Office must be held to account for what went wrong, why repeated warnings were ignored and the harm caused to members.”

It added that its “immediate concern is ensuring Capita’s financial difficulties do not further destabilise the service or disrupt pension payments”.

“Changing the CEO does not remove responsibility for what happened on his watch,” the Civil Service Campaigns Group said.

Pension disaster

In 2023, the Cabinet Office awarded Capita a seven-year contract worth £239m for the administration of the CSPS, which has 1.7 million members. The takeover from the previous administrator, MyCSP, took place on 1 December 2025. 

Since it took on the contract, Capita has failed to meet its delivery promises, leaving claimants in severe financial difficulties. Thousands of retired civil servants are affected by the CSPS problems – some have waited nearly a year for their pensions, and at least one has been forced to use a food bank.

Capita has admitted it is set to lose money on the contract, with pressure mounting on the organisation, which is heavily reliant on public sector business, due to the government’s current insourcing plans combined with its much-publicised failures.

In January 2026, just a month after Capita took over from MyCSP and following a litany of problems, a troubleshooter stepped in from HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) to lead an “urgent recovery plan”, which included 150 staff being moved temporarily from HMRC to the service.

Disaster after disaster has now prompted the government to make the decision to bring the service in-house, but no timeline has been given.
